description: We are a passionate multidisciplinary team from SBTU Rocket and Propulsion Society, launching as one of our club's inaugural competition squads! Our team combines Aircraft Engineering (Esra Acar, 4th yr; Mustafa Alp Karaviran, 3rd yr), Computer Engineering (Enes Aslantaş), and Chemical Engineering (İbrahim Şentürk, prep). Driven by space exploration, propulsion, and software, we turn bold ideas into working prototypes. Looking for teammates skilled in AI/Data Science, UI/UX, or Graphic Design.
summary:
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we, the SBTU Rocket and Propulsion Team, developed the "Left-Behind League" web application. We built a dynamic platform designed to gamify space education for children through a five-step interactive journey: Meet, Explore, Find, Play, and Create. Our project features 3D models of spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars, a custom hero builder, and an immersive Moon/Mars simulation.

We addressed the challenge of telling the story of discarded space equipment by turning these forgotten rovers and landers into "heroes." Instead of viewing them as space junk, children can interact with their real data, explore their landing sites, and step into their mission moments.

By making complex mission histories interactive and understandable, we ensure that space education is accessible to everyone. Through our website, we inspire the next generation of space explorers, ensuring no hero—and no child—is left behind.
details:
The Left-Behind League turns the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars into heroes that kids can meet, explore and play with.

Website: https://eesracarr48.github.io/Left_Behind_League/

What it does and how it works

Instead of “space junk,” children discover that rovers like Spirit, landers like Phoenix and the Ingenuity helicopter outlived their missions and changed what we know about space. The site is a five-step journey:

Meet: 13 hero cards, each opening an info card with dates, what the machine taught us, where it is today, and links to NASA sources. An Explore Space section covers the Moon, Mars and the “firsts.”

Find: a map shows where each machine is today; a 3D hangar lets kids rotate and inspect the models.

Play (our MVP): a 3D simulation on two surfaces, the Moon and Mars. Kids design their own avatar, walk on the surface, find 16 real NASA machines through an explorer’s log, read each machine’s story when they get close, and call, ride and drive a rover.

Create: kids compare their height with the machines, design their own hero and download its card as a PNG, and find their “space twin” in a short quiz.

Think: Mission Moments shows real problems the machines faced and asks “What would you do?” before revealing NASA’s solution.

Benefits and intended impact

Space feels distant to many children, and most resources about these missions are text-heavy. Our goal is to make kids love space while they learn: they explore, play and create instead of only reading. They also take something home: a photo next to a rover or their own hero card. The site works in English and Turkish, so it also reaches children who don’t speak English.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages

Three.js for the 3D simulation

Leaflet with NASA Trek layers for the maps

Sketchfab embeds for 3D models

SVG and Canvas for size comparison and PNG export

NASA data: NSSDC catalog, NASA Science and NASA/JPL pages, NASA Trek, GISS Mars24

An AI assistant helped us write and debug code; hero illustrations are AI-generated and labeled on the site

Our own laptops and phones for development and mobile testing

How it is creative

We tell the story through characters: every machine has a nickname, a superpower and a weak spot, like a game hero. The Moon and Mars each have their own light and dark theme in both the site and the simulation. Kids put themselves inside the story by walking next to the machines, measuring themselves against them and designing their own.

Factors we considered

Every fact comes from NASA sources and is linked. We used simple language and learning through play. The site needs no installation, has a mobile view with touch controls, and works in two languages. AI-generated images are clearly labeled.
